title: A Radical Way To Transform Difficult Students https://smartclassroommanagement.com/2017/04/29/a-radical-way-to-transform-difficult-students/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Michael Linsin offers a strategy for the chronically disruptive student who resists all typical consequences: consciously changing how the teacher thinks and feels about that student. He argues that negative feelings, even carefully hidden ones, are perceptible to students through subtle cues in tone, body language, and demeanor, and that this perceived dislike destroys a teacher's leverage to influence behavior. Rather than focusing further on consequences, Linsin recommends a deliberate mental choice to see only the best in the student, arguing that genuine warmth triggers reciprocity and can produce surprisingly fast behavioral improvement. He supports the claim with an analogy to how even infants can sense insincere affection, and frames the shift as requiring real willpower rather than sentimentality. The piece closes by describing this as an act of leadership capable of reaching students other teachers have written off.
points: For chronically disruptive students who resist standard consequences, the recommended intervention is changing the teacher's internal feelings toward the student, not adding more consequences.
Negative feelings toward a student, even carefully hidden, are perceptible to students through subtle tone, body language, and demeanor cues.
When mutual likability is absent between teacher and student, the teacher loses nearly all leverage to influence that student's behavior.
The intervention is a deliberate, effortful mental choice to see only the best in the student, not a spontaneous feeling.
Genuine warmth toward a difficult student triggers reciprocity, often producing surprisingly fast behavioral improvement once the student senses real acceptance.
quotes: You spend more time dealing with them than any ten students put together. You think about them in your off hours. You talk about them with your spouse.
Well, the big secret is that they know how you feel about them, even if you've done your Meryl-Streep best pretending otherwise.
Children are astute, even psychic, judges of how adults perceive them. Far more than we give them credit for.
When there is an absence of mutual likability between you and your most challenging students, you lose nearly all of your leverage to influence their behavior.
You make a conscious decision that, no matter what they do or how they behave or how many times they disrupt your class, you’re going to see only the best in them.
It triggers the Law of Reciprocity and causes in them a desire to please you and behave for you.
